stem: A nurse is teaching a new parent how to care for a normal umbilical cord stump at home. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.A: Clean the stump routinely with rubbing alcohol after diaper changes and keep it covered with dry gauze until separation.
options.B: Keep it clean and dry, fold the diaper below it, and use sponge baths until it falls off.
options.C: Apply petroleum jelly routinely so the stump remains moist until separation.
options.D: Begin routine tub baths while the stump is attached as long as it is dried afterward.

rationale: American Academy of Pediatrics HealthyChildren guidance recommends dry cord care for a normal stump: keep it clean and dry, fold the diaper below the cord to promote air exposure, and use sponge baths rather than tub baths until the cord separates. Routine rubbing alcohol is not recommended unless specifically instructed. Therefore B is correct.
educational_objective: Teach routine dry umbilical-cord care: keep the stump clean and dry, keep the diaper below it, and use sponge baths until separation.

source_original.stem: A nurse is teaching a new parent how to care for a normal umbilical cord stump at home. Which instruction is most appropriate?

options.A: Clean the stump routinely with rubbing alcohol after diaper changes and keep it covered with dry gauze until separation.
options.B: Keep it clean and dry, fold the diaper below it, and use sponge baths until it falls off.
options.C: Apply petroleum jelly routinely so the stump remains moist until separation.
options.D: Begin routine tub baths while the stump is attached as long as it is dried afterward.

source_original.rationale: AAP guidance recommends dry cord care: keep the stump clean and dry, fold the diaper below it to promote air exposure, and use sponge baths until the cord separates. Option B therefore best reflects routine home care. Option A adds routine alcohol and gauze that are not recommended for an uncomplicated stump. Option C keeps the stump moist and covered, contrary to dry-cord care. Option D introduces tub bathing while the stump remains attached rather than using sponge baths.
source_original.source_detail: American Academy of Pediatrics HealthyChildren.org — Umbilical Cord Symptoms/Care: keep stump clean/dry, fold diaper below for air contact, use sponge baths until cord falls off; avoid routine rubbing alcohol. correction_summary: No clinical correction was required. The source locator was expanded to the exact AAP dry-cord-care, bathing, and diaper sections, and the rationale was tightened to avoid adding unsupported treatment beyond routine care.

audit_findings.exact_locator: Normal Dry Cord Care, Bathing, and Fold Diaper Down sections directly support every element of the keyed instruction.
audit_findings.claim_audit: No separation-time estimate, antiseptic exception beyond clinician instruction, or infection-treatment claim was required for the answer.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because routine rubbing alcohol is not recommended and routine gauze coverage conflicts with air/dry care.
distractor_audit.B: Correct and directly matches AAP guidance.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because routine moist occlusive care is contrary to keeping the stump dry.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because AAP recommends avoiding tub baths and using sponge baths until separation.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B combines all recommended routine-care elements.
audit_findings.cueing: All choices are home-care instructions of comparable detail.
audit_findings.blueprint: Fits Health Promotion and Maintenance through newborn-care teaching.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Second-pass review checked current AAP advice on alcohol, bathing, and diaper positioning; no competing answer remains.
